z1.text: For a long time, the wound continued to burn. Many a traveller Siddhartha had to ferry across the river who was accompanied by a son or a daughter, and he saw none of them without envying him, without thinking: "So many, so many thousands possess this sweetest of good fortunes—why don't I? Even bad people, even thieves and robbers have children and love them, and are being loved by them, all except for me." Thus simply, thus without reason he now thought, thus similar to the childlike people he had become.

z2.text: Differently than before, he now looked upon people, less smart, less proud, but instead warmer, more curious, more involved. When he ferried travellers of the ordinary kind, childlike people, businessmen, warriors, women, these people did not seem alien to him as they used to: he understood them, he understood and shared their life, which was not guided by thoughts and insight, but solely by urges and wishes, he felt like them.

z3.text: Worthy of love and admiration were these people in their blind loyalty, their blind strength and tenacity. They lacked nothing, there was nothing the knowledgeable one, the thinker, had to put him above them except for one little thing, a single, tiny, small thing: the consciousness, the conscious thought of the oneness of all life. And Siddhartha even doubted in many an hour, whether this knowledge, this thought was to be valued thus highly, whether it might not also perhaps be a childish idea of the thinking people, of the thinking and childlike people.

z4.text: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was. It was nothing but a readiness of the soul, an ability, a secret art, to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness, to be able to feel and inhale the oneness. Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva's old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.

z5.text: And one day, when the wound burned violently, Siddhartha ferried across the river, driven by a yearning, got off the boat and was willing to go to the city and to look for his son. The river flowed softly and quietly, it was the dry season, but its voice sounded strange: it laughed! It laughed clearly. The river laughed, it laughed brightly and clearly at the old ferryman. Siddhartha stopped, he bent over the water, in order to hear even better, and he saw his face reflected in the quietly moving waters, and in this reflected face there was something, which reminded him, something he had forgotten, and as he thought about it, he found it: this face resembled another face, which he used to know and love and also fear. It resembled his father's face, the Brahmin.

z6.text: And he remembered how he, a long time ago, as a young man, had forced his father to let him go to the penitents, how he had bade his farewell to him, how he had gone and had never come back. Had his father not also suffered the same pain for him, which he now suffered for his son? Had his father not long since died, alone, without having seen his son again? Did he not have to expect the same fate for himself? Was it not a comedy, a strange and stupid matter, this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?

z7.text: While he spoke, spoke for a long time, while Vasudeva was listening with a quiet face, Vasudeva's listening gave Siddhartha a stronger sensation than ever before, he sensed how his pain, his fears flowed over to him, how his secret hope flowed over, came back at him from his counterpart. To show his wound to this listener was the same as bathing it in the river, until it had cooled and become one with the river. While he was still speaking, still admitting and confessing, Siddhartha felt more and more that this was no longer Vasudeva, no longer a human being, who was listening to him, that this motionless listener was absorbing his confession into himself like a tree the rain, that this motionless man was the river itself, that he was God himself, that he was the eternal itself.

z8.text: They listened. Softly sounded the river, singing in many voices. Siddhartha looked into the water, and images appeared to him in the moving water: his father appeared, lonely, mourning for his son; he himself appeared, lonely, he also being tied with the bondage of yearning to his distant son; his son appeared, lonely as well, the boy, greedily rushing along the burning course of his young wishes, each one heading for his goal, each one obsessed by the goal, each one suffering. The river sang with a voice of suffering, longingly it sang, longingly, it flowed towards its goal, lamentingly its voice sang.

z9.text: Siddhartha listened. He was now nothing but a listener, completely concentrated on listening, completely empty, he felt, that he had now finished learning to listen. Often before, he had heard all this, these many voices in the river, today it sounded new. Already, he could no longer tell the many voices apart, not the happy ones from the weeping ones, not the ones of children from those of men, they all belonged together, the lamentation of yearning and the laughter of the knowledgeable one, the scream of rage and the moaning of the dying ones, everything was one, everything was intertwined and connected, entangled a thousand times. And everything together, all voices, all goals, all yearning, all suffering, all pleasure, all that was good and evil, all of this together was the world. All of it together was the flow of events, was the music of life.

z10.text: Brightly, Vasudeva's smile was shining, floating radiantly over all the wrinkles of his old face, as the Om was floating in the air over all the voices of the river. Brightly his smile was shining, when he looked at his friend, and brightly the same smile was now starting to shine on Siddhartha's face as well. His wound blossomed, his suffering was shining, his self had flown into the oneness. In this hour, Siddhartha stopped fighting his fate, stopped suffering. On his face flourished the cheerfulness of a knowledge, which is no longer opposed by any will, which knows perfection, which is in agreement with the flow of events, with the current of life, full of sympathy for the pain of others, full of sympathy for the pleasure of others, devoted to the flow, belonging to the oneness.

z11.text: I've been waiting for this hour, my dear. Now that it has come, let me leave. For a long time, I've been waiting for this hour; for a long time, I've been Vasudeva the ferryman. Now it's enough. Farewell, hut, farewell, river, farewell, Siddhartha!" Siddhartha made a deep bow before him who bid his farewell. "I've known it," he said quietly. "You'll go into the forests?" "I'm going into the forests, I'm going into the oneness," spoke Vasudeva with a bright smile. With a bright smile, he left; Siddhartha watched him leaving. With deep joy, with deep solemnity he watched him leave, saw his steps full of peace, saw his head full of lustre, saw his body full of light.

z12.text: Vasudeva was sitting in the hut and weaving a basket. He no longer used the ferryboat, his eyes were starting to get weak, and not just his eyes; his arms and hands as well. Unchanged and flourishing was only the joy and the cheerful benevolence of his face. Siddhartha sat down next to the old man, slowly he started talking. What they had never talked about, he now told him of, of his walk to the city, at that time, of the burning wound, of his envy at the sight of happy fathers, of his knowledge of the foolishness of such wishes, of his futile fight against them. He reported everything, he was able to say everything, even the most embarrassing parts, everything could be said, everything shown, everything he could tell.

z14.text: And everything together, all voices, all goals, all yearning, all suffering, all pleasure, all that was good and evil, all of this together was the world. All of it together was the flow of events, was the music of life. And when Siddhartha was listening attentively to this river, this song of a thousand voices, when he neither listened to the suffering nor the laughter, when he did not tie his soul to any particular voice and submerged his self into it, but when he heard them all, perceived the whole, the oneness, then the great song of the thousand voices consisted of a single word, which was Om: the perfection.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha becomes a thief to provide for himself.
Siddhartha finds his lost son among the travellers.
Siddhartha stops ferrying travellers because he can no longer bear to see their happy children.
Grieving for his son, Siddhartha envies other parents and grows like the childlike people.
A.explanation: He envies every traveller with a child, and "thus similar to the childlike people he had become." He keeps ferrying them, so he does not stop. His son is not found. He mentions thieves who love their children, but he does not become one.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what was Vasudeva doing when Siddhartha returned?
options: Weaving a basket in the hut
Sleeping on his mat
Ferrying travellers across the river
Cooking rice for supper
A.explanation: The passage says "Vasudeva was sitting in the hut and weaving a basket." He "no longer used the ferryboat," so ferrying is wrong. Cooking and sleeping are not mentioned here; he is weaving. Vasudeva has stopped ferrying because his eyes and hands have grown weak with age.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "tenacity" most nearly means
options: persistence
cruelty
cleverness
weakness
A.explanation: Paired with "blind strength" and with their stubborn effort, tenacity means persistence. Weakness and giving up are the opposite. "Cleverness" is not what is praised; the thinkers have that. "Cruelty" is not suggested; the passage calls them "worthy of love." The word describes the stubborn strength the worldly people show in pursuing their goals.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now sees that his father
options: was a cruel and hard man
is still alive and waiting for him
suffered for him as he now suffers for his son
was glad to see him leave and soon forgot him entirely
A.explanation: He asks, "Had his father not also suffered the same pain for him, which he now suffered for his son?" Being glad and forgetting him contradicts that. The father "had... long since died." Nothing calls him cruel. He realizes his father once felt the same pain he now feels for his runaway son.

A.prompt: Why does Vasudeva leave at this moment?
options: He wants to go and find the boy.
The hour he had waited for has come.
He has grown too old to row the boat.
He is angry at Siddhartha's long grief.
A.explanation: Vasudeva says, "I've been waiting for this hour, my dear. Now that it has come, let me leave." He is not angry; he smiles. His weakness is real but not his reason here. He goes "into the oneness," not after the boy.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "With a bright smile, he left; Siddhartha watched him leaving."
"I'm going into the forests, I'm going into the oneness,"
"Siddhartha made a deep bow before him who bid his farewell."
"I've been waiting for this hour, my dear. Now that it has come, let me leave."
A.explanation: Only "I've been waiting for this hour... let me leave" gives his reason. "With a bright smile, he left" describes his departure. The bow is Siddhartha's response. "I'm going into the forests" says where Vasudeva is going, not why he leaves at this hour.

A.prompt: The repeated word "lonely" in the images of father, self and son mainly serves to
options: show that each man lives far from any town or village
show the same longing repeated in each generation
show that all three men are angry
describe the river's banks and trees
A.explanation: Each image is "lonely," each "heading for his goal... suffering," so the same longing repeats across his father, Siddhartha himself, and his son. Living far from towns is not the point. The banks are not described. Loneliness and longing, not anger, are stressed.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha forgets the goal of his long search.
Siddhartha decides that wisdom means learning as many teachings as possible from many different teachers.
Siddhartha slowly comes to see wisdom as a readiness to feel the oneness of all things.
Vasudeva teaches Siddhartha a lesson in many careful words.
A.explanation: Wisdom "was nothing but a readiness of the soul... to feel and inhale the oneness." Collecting teachings is his old path. Vasudeva teaches with his "old, childlike face," not words. The passage names "the goal of his long search," so he has not forgotten it.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what did the river do?
options: It flooded its banks.
It became silent.
It froze.
It laughed.
A.explanation: "The river laughed, it laughed brightly and clearly at the old ferryman." It "flowed softly and quietly," so no flood. It was not silent; it laughed. It was "the dry season," and no freezing is mentioned. The river's laughter mocks his foolish wish to follow his son.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "alien" most nearly means
options: from outer space
hostile
strange and foreign
familiar
A.explanation: People "did not seem alien to him as they used to: he understood them," so alien means strange and foreign. "From outer space" is a modern sense that does not fit. "Hostile" goes too far. "Familiar" is what they have now become.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that, as he confides in Vasudeva, Siddhartha
options: feels he is being heard by something greater than a man
falls asleep while he is still talking
regrets telling his secrets to Vasudeva
grows impatient because Vasudeva does not answer his questions
A.explanation: He felt that this was no longer Vasudeva, no longer a man, but the river or God himself. He is not impatient; he talks on and on. No regret is shown. He keeps speaking, so he does not sleep. He feels that Vasudeva has become the river, or even God, listening to him.

A.prompt: The comparison "like a tree the rain" suggests that Vasudeva
options: grows tall and strong like a tree
takes in Siddhartha's words quietly and completely
is old, weak and dying
refuses to hear the confession and turns away from him
A.explanation: The "motionless listener was absorbing his confession into himself like a tree the rain," taking it in quietly and fully. He does not refuse; he absorbs. Age is not the point of this comparison. Growing tall is not meant. The image shows Vasudeva absorbing the confession silently and fully.

B.prompt: According to the passage, the great song of a thousand voices consisted of what single word?
options: Atman
Brahman
Sansara
Om
B.explanation: When he "heard them all, perceived the whole, the oneness," then "the great song of the thousand voices consisted of a single word, which was Om." Atman and Brahman are words from his youth but not the word here. Sansara, the world of cycles, is not named. The single word Om joins all the river's voices into one.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "flourished" most nearly means
options: withered
bloomed
spoke
hid
B.explanation: "On his face flourished the cheerfulness of a knowledge," so it bloomed or thrived. "Withered" is the opposite. Cheerfulness that "flourished" on his face is visible, not hidden. "Spoke" does not fit. The word describes the cheerful knowledge that now shows on his face.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now understands ordinary people because he
options: shares their urges and wishes himself
has become rich again
pities them
has studied them carefully from a distance
B.explanation: "He understood and shared their life... he felt like them." Studying from a distance was his old way. Pity is not stated; he "felt like them." He is a poor ferryman, not rich. He now shares the urges and wishes of ordinary people, so he understands them.

B.prompt: What changes in Siddhartha in this hour?
options: He stops fighting his fate.
He leaves the ferry for good.
He decides to fetch his son home by force.
He grows angry with Vasudeva.
B.explanation: "In this hour, Siddhartha stopped fighting his fate, stopped suffering." He does not decide to fetch his son. Vasudeva leaves, not Siddhartha. He smiles with Vasudeva, so no anger. From this hour he no longer resists his fate, and his suffering stops.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "as the Om was floating in the air over all the voices of the river"
"full of sympathy for the pain of others"
"In this hour, Siddhartha stopped fighting his fate, stopped suffering."
"Brightly, Vasudeva's smile was shining, floating radiantly over all the wrinkles of his old face"
B.explanation: Only "stopped fighting his fate, stopped suffering" states the change. Vasudeva's shining smile describes Vasudeva. "Full of sympathy for the pain of others" describes the new knowledge, not the change itself. The Om line describes the river's voices. The chosen line states directly that he stopped fighting his fate.

B.prompt: The series of questions about his father mainly serves to
options: show that he has forgotten his father
praise his father's wisdom
build his realization that the same pain is repeating
ask Vasudeva where his father is buried
B.explanation: "Had his father not also suffered...? Did he not have to expect the same fate...?" lead to "this repetition." They are thoughts, not questions to Vasudeva. He remembers his father clearly. They concern suffering, not wisdom. The questions lead him to see his own pain as a repetition of his father's.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Vasudeva weaves a basket for the boy.
Siddhartha tells Vasudeva everything, even the most embarrassing parts.
Vasudeva tells Siddhartha his own life story.
Siddhartha hides his failed trip to the city from Vasudeva out of shame.
B.explanation: "He reported everything, he was able to say everything, even the most embarrassing parts." He does not hide the trip; he tells "of his walk to the city." Vasudeva listens rather than tells. The basket is not for the boy.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "solemnity" most nearly means
options: hurry
foolishness
anger
seriousness
B.explanation: He watched "with deep joy, with deep solemnity," a grave, serious feeling at a great farewell. Foolishness is the opposite. Anger and hurry do not fit his calm watching. The word describes the grave and serious feeling with which he watches Vasudeva leave.

B.prompt: The list "the lamentation of yearning and the laughter of the knowledgeable one, the scream of rage and the moaning of the dying ones" mainly serves to
options: show that the river is dangerous
name the travellers who once crossed the river
describe Vasudeva
show opposite voices merging into one whole
B.explanation: The list pairs opposites that "all belonged together... everything was one." They are voices, not named travellers. The river is not shown as dangerous. Vasudeva is not described in this list. The list shows that all these opposite voices together form one song.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now doubts whether
options: the thinker's awareness of oneness truly sets him above others
Vasudeva is truly as wise as he seems
the river can really speak to people
the worldly people deserve to live at all
B.explanation: He "doubted in many an hour, whether this knowledge... was to be valued thus highly." He calls the people "worthy of love," so no doubt about their worth. The river is not discussed here. Vasudeva is not mentioned. He now doubts whether his awareness of oneness truly makes him better than the people.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's quoted thought "why don't I?" mainly reveals
options: his anger at Vasudeva for keeping the boy from him
his pride in being a thinker
the simple, childlike envy he now feels
his hope for riches
B.explanation: He thinks "So many, so many thousands possess this sweetest of good fortunes—why don't I?" "Thus simply, thus without reason" shows childlike envy. Vasudeva is not blamed. Pride and riches are not involved. The simple question shows how childlike his envy of other parents has become.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 explain the resemblance Siddhartha notices in Passage 1?
options: It shows him deciding that the face was a trick of the light.
It shows him seeing his own pain as a repetition of his father's.
It shows that his father has come to the river to find him.
It shows him laughing at his father.
B.explanation: In Passage 1 his face resembles his father's; in Passage 2 he recalls leaving his father and asks if his father "suffered the same pain." His father "had... long since died." He takes the resemblance seriously. He does not laugh at his father.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: The river falls silent at last and speaks no more.
Siddhartha stops listening to the river and leaves it.
When Siddhartha hears all the river's voices together, they become a single Om.
Siddhartha learns to tell apart every one of the river's voices, the happy from the sad.
C.explanation: When he "heard them all, perceived the whole, the oneness," the song "consisted of a single word, which was Om." He does not tell the voices apart; he hears them "all voices... together." The river is full of voices, so it does not fall silent. He is "listening attentively," not leaving.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's grief has
options: ended for good
made him hate children
made him more like ordinary people
made him wiser than other fathers
C.explanation: "Thus simply, thus without reason he now thought, thus similar to the childlike people he had become." He does not feel wiser. He envies parents, not hates children. "The wound continued to burn," so it has not ended. His grief brings him closer to the childlike people he used to look down on.

C.prompt: The comparison of Vasudeva's smile to "the Om... floating in the air over all the voices of the river" mainly serves to
options: link his smile with the oneness Siddhartha has just heard
show that Vasudeva has begun to sing along with the river
show that the river is loud
describe the weather
C.explanation: His smile floats over his wrinkles "as the Om was floating... over all the voices," linking it to oneness. He is silent, not singing. No weather is described. The comparison concerns unity, not loudness. The comparison links Vasudeva's smile with the Om that joins all voices.

C.prompt: What does Siddhartha come to suspect about his situation?
options: The same pain is repeating in a circle.
His father is still alive.
The river is lying to him.
His son will come back tomorrow, as he once came back.
C.explanation: He asks, "Was it not a comedy... this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?" He himself "had never come back," so expecting the boy back reverses the pattern. His father "had... long since died." He does not call the river a liar.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Had his father not long since died, alone, without having seen his son again?"
"Was it not a comedy, a strange and stupid matter, this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?"
"how he had bade his farewell to him, how he had gone"
"And he remembered how he, a long time ago, as a young man, had forced his father to let him go"
C.explanation: Only the "repetition... fateful circle" line names his suspicion. The "forced his father" line recalls the past. "Bade his farewell" also recalls the past. "Long since died" adds a fact about his father, not the pattern itself. The chosen line names the repetition he now suspects in his own life.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "readiness" most nearly means
options: quickness of a runner's start
willingness and preparation
wealth
tiredness
C.explanation: Wisdom was "a readiness of the soul, an ability... to think every moment... the thought of oneness," so it means prepared willingness. Speed is a different sense. Tiredness and wealth do not fit an ability of the soul. The word describes the readiness of the soul to feel the oneness of all life.

C.prompt: The words "His wound blossomed, his suffering was shining" suggest that his pain
options: was transformed into something beautiful
was cured by medicine
grew worse and spread through his whole body
was forgotten
C.explanation: A wound that "blossomed" and suffering that is "shining" have been transformed into something beautiful, as hoped earlier. The pain does not grow worse. It is transformed, not forgotten. No medicine is involved. The image shows his pain transformed into something bright and beautiful.

C.prompt: Vasudeva's farewell suggests that his work as ferryman was
options: unfinished and left to Siddhartha
a punishment for old sins
a burden he hated and was glad to finally escape
complete once Siddhartha reached this understanding
C.explanation: He says "I've been waiting for this hour... for a long time, I've been Vasudeva the ferryman. Now it's enough," so his task is complete. He leaves "with a bright smile," not escaping a burden he hated. Nothing suggests it was unfinished or a punishment.

C.prompt: The repetition of "longingly" in the final sentence mainly serves to
options: show that the river is drying up in the heat
show the river's joy
stress the yearning in the river's song
describe the boat on the water
C.explanation: "Longingly it sang, longingly, it flowed towards its goal" stresses yearning. No drying is mentioned. The boat is not described. The song is "a voice of suffering," not joy. The repetition stresses how the river's voice longs for its goal.

C.prompt: The narration in the passage mainly shows
options: a conversation with the boy
the narrator's criticism of Siddhartha
Vasudeva's own private thoughts and judgments about the confession
Siddhartha's changing perception of Vasudeva as he speaks
C.explanation: The passage follows what Siddhartha "felt" and "sensed": that Vasudeva was "the river itself... God himself." Vasudeva's thoughts are not given. The boy is absent. The narrator does not criticize. The narration follows Siddhartha's growing sense that Vasudeva is the river itself.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 resolve the river's song in Passage 1?
options: The suffering voices fall silent and only laughter remains.
Passage 2 shows Siddhartha leaving the river.
Passage 2 shows the river drying up.
The voices of suffering join all others into one Om.
C.explanation: Passage 1 hears "a voice of suffering"; in Passage 2, joy and suffering "all belonged together" and "everything was one." Suffering does not fall silent. The river does not dry up. He stays, listening. Passage 2 joins the river's sad and joyful voices into one Om.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 relate to the change in Passage 1?
options: It shows Vasudeva leaving the hut for the forest.
It names the oneness that lets him feel close to ordinary people.
It shows him rejecting ordinary people as foolish once more, as before.
It describes the city and its crowded streets.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows him understanding ordinary people; Passage 2 defines wisdom as feeling "the oneness," which underlies that closeness. He does not reject them. The city is not described. Vasudeva's face appears, but he does not leave here. Passage 2 explains the oneness behind his new closeness to ordinary people.
